clue.text: Pass salt — that's the right thing to do

parts.note: to salt food is to season it

parts.words: that's the right thing to do
parts.note: 'just the ticket' is an idiom for exactly the right thing

explanation.surface: At the dinner table, passing the salt when asked is simply good manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' looks like a verb at the table; it is a noun, the card that lets you travel. 'The ticket' is old British slang for the correct or proper thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pass valid for travel or entry over a whole period is the long-term ticket commuters and fans buy.

clue.text: The way in, round part of the plant, to the candle-maker

indicators.note: the first pieces wrap themselves round the plant part, so they act as a container

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
taken as written
an ear is the seed-bearing head of a cereal plant such as corn

explanation.surface: Directions to a candle-maker's workshop: go in, round part of the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' makes the first pieces wrap the plant part. The definition is loose: the answer is what the candle-maker knows as a raw material for candles.
explanation.definitionFit: A white fatty compound from animal or vegetable fats, long used as the main ingredient in making candles.

clue.text: Judge a royal corgi perhaps

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for royal (as in RN, Royal Navy)
a corgi, a small snappy dog, is an example of one that bites

explanation.surface: Is it fair to call a royal corgi a judge? The Queen's dogs were famous.
explanation.walkthrough: The corgi is the Queen's famous breed, which sets the royal scene; here it is just an example of a dog that nips. 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbiter is a referee or umpire who settles disputes, so a synonym for a judge.

clue.text: Epithet for the eyes of the exceptionally vigilant

definitions.text: Epithet for the eyes of the exceptionally vigilant

parts.words: Epithet for the eyes of the exceptionally vigilant
parts.note: a very watchful person is said to have eyes in the back of the head, so their eyes would be described by the adjective for that region of the skull

explanation.surface: A writer hunts for the right adjective to describe a super-alert lookout's eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'eyes in the back of one's head' is taken literally: the anatomical adjective for the back of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective names the rear part of the skull, where the idiom places a watchful person's extra eyes.

clue.text: Experience a smack

definitions.meaning: to experience something, as in 'get a sample of life'
a smack is a slight flavour, as in 'a smack of garlic'

explanation.definitionFit: To try or undergo something is to sample it, and a smack is a faint savour of flavour.

clue.text: Solicit orders for the sales, say

indicators.note: say tells us the cloth's name is heard, standing for a word spelt differently

parts.note: 'sales' sounds like sails, and sails are made of the heavy cloth used for them

explanation.surface: A salesman knocks on doors drumming up orders for the shop's sales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sales' sounds like sails, whose cloth is CANVAS; 'say' signals that CANVAS sounds the same as the answer, which takes a second S.
explanation.definitionFit: To canvass is to go round seeking votes, opinions or custom, so to solicit business.

clue.text: Optical solution is an illusion

definitions.meaning: a lotion for bathing tired or sore eyes
a deception or nonsense meant to mislead, as in 'it's all a sham'

explanation.definitionFit: Literally a lotion to bathe sore eyes; figuratively talk meant to deceive, humbug or a sham.

clue.text: Epithet can go astray, describing development of a disease

indicators.note: letters that go astray wander out of place and are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A poorly chosen adjective can mislead when doctors describe how an illness progresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astray' rearranges EPITHET + CANGO, twelve letters, into the answer. 'Epithet' reads like literary talk but is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective is the medical term for how illness arises and progresses in the body.

clue.text: Still enough to becalm one, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Is this calm enough to leave a sailor becalmed?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adjective meaning calm, matching 'becalm'; it is a noun, an apparatus for distilling. 'perhaps' rearranges BECALM + I.
explanation.definitionFit: An alembic is an old distilling apparatus, the alchemist's vessel for purifying liquids.

clue.text: Ultraviolet ray used in the tanning process

definitions.text: Ultraviolet ray used in the tanning process

parts.words: Ultraviolet ray used in the tanning process
parts.note: reads like leather-tanning chemistry or a sunbed lamp, but means the natural light that browns skin on a beach

explanation.surface: A technical note on the radiation used in a tannery or salon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tanning' suggests leather or a tanning salon; the tanning meant is getting a suntan outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaft of sunlight, which carries the radiation that browns skin, is the ray behind a suntan.

clue.text: Abstract the iron, for example, out of a medicine

indicators.note: the metal lies out of, that is outside, the medicine, so it wraps round it

parts.note: iron is an example of a metal
taken as written
physic is an old word for medicine

explanation.surface: Instructions to extract the iron from a tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abstract' looks like a verb meaning extract; it is the adjective. 'out of' puts METAL outside A PHYSIC. 'Physic' is an old word for a medicinal drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Metaphysical means concerned with abstract philosophical ideas beyond the physical world.

clue.text: Hire-purchase includes a way to get this type of car

indicators.note: includes means the hire-purchase letters take the rest inside them

parts.note: taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way
taken as written

explanation.surface: Buying a car on credit is the route to getting one.
explanation.walkthrough: Hire-purchase is the British term for buying on instalments. 'includes' puts the way and its neighbours inside the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A car with a rigid roof, often a detachable one on a sports model, rather than a soft folding top.

clue.text: A patent error — shocking!

indicators.note: an error puts things wrong, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A glaring mistake: how scandalous!
explanation.walkthrough: 'A patent error' reads as 'an obvious mistake'; 'error' rearranges A PATENT. The answer is a French word adopted in English.
explanation.definitionFit: From French épater, to startle; it describes something that astonishes or scandalises the respectable.

clue.text: Left by the river, he's had it

parts.note: left means departed, gone
R is the abbreviation for river on maps

explanation.surface: A man abandoned on the riverbank is done for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'he's had it' is the definition: a person beyond saving.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone doomed or beyond hope is a lost cause, as in 'he's a dead man'.

clue.text: Thin spars to move from one boat to another

indicators.note: letters set to move change places, so the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Slender masts need shifting from one vessel to another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to move' rearranges THIN SPARS. Read with 'to move', the definition phrase describes shifting cargo between vessels, the action the verb names.
explanation.definitionFit: To transfer cargo or passengers from one ship to another vessel, often in mid-voyage.

clue.text: You could be unlucky to shoot such a score, of course

definitions.text: You could be unlucky to shoot such
definitions.meaning: a seabird that, in Coleridge's poem of the Ancient Mariner, brings bad luck on the sailor who shoots it
in golf, a score of three under par on one hole of the course

explanation.definitionFit: The great seabird brings ill luck to the mariner who kills it, and in golf it names three under par on a hole.

clue.text: Dark suit required for this place of entertainment

parts.note: the dark is night-time
clubs is one of the four suits in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A dark suit is the dress code for this venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark suit' reads as formal evening wear; it splits into darkness and a card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A late-opening venue for drinking, music and dancing after dark.

clue.text: Grating familiar to rail travellers

parts.note: the grille of a station ticket window, the French name for it known to travellers on the continent

explanation.surface: Something harsh-sounding that train passengers know well, like squealing brakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grating' suggests an irritating noise; it is a grille, the barred hatch at a ticket office, a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hatch or grille in a wall, especially a station ticket-office window, a French loanword.

clue.text: Clumsy idiot gives cat a dish of cream

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
a fool is a dessert of fruit purée folded into cream

explanation.surface: A bumbling fool hands the cat a saucer of cream.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British pudding of stewed fruit mixed with cream, as in gooseberry fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffoon or foolish person, an old word for a silly clown.

clue.text: One easily persuaded to impose the Treasury's limits

parts.note: to impose is to put, as in 'put a tax on'

indicators.note: limits are the boundaries of the word, so its first and last letters are taken

explanation.surface: A pliable minister bows to the Treasury's spending caps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'limits' takes T and Y, the first and last letters of 'Treasury'. 'Putty in someone's hands' is the idiom behind the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone easily moulded is like soft filler compound, as in 'putty in her hands'.

clue.text: Fix old boy up with dummy pill

parts.note: to fix something is to place it

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: Set up the old chap with a fake tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses OB to give BO in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmless sham tablet given for psychological effect or as a control in a drug trial.

clue.text: Passage conveying movement

definitions.meaning: passage as in a journey or crossing from one place to another
the carrying of goods or people, as in goods in shipment

explanation.definitionFit: It means both a journey across and the conveyance of goods or people from one place to another.

clue.text: He hopes a change of view will prove beneficial

definitions.text: He hopes a change of view will prove beneficial

parts.words: He hopes a change of view will prove beneficial
parts.note: reads like a holidaymaker seeking a change of scenery, but means a politician who shifts opinions for advantage

explanation.surface: A convalescent hopes new scenery will do him good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change of view' suggests new scenery; it means changing one's opinions. Historically the word named politicians who adjusted their sails to the prevailing wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat who shifts political allegiance to suit the times, from trimming sails to the wind.

clue.text: Battered trees can be put back in position

indicators.note: battered means knocked about, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Trees knocked down in a storm can be replanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' rearranges TREES.
explanation.definitionFit: To set again, restoring something such as a bone to its proper place.

clue.text: Flower receptacles in the women's apartments

definitions.meaning: the receptacle is the part of a flower stalk bearing the floral organs
in ancient Greek houses, the inner rooms set aside for women

explanation.definitionFit: Plural of a Greek-derived word for an inner chamber: botanically the floral receptacle, historically the women's quarters.

clue.text: Accountant takes funny people into partnership

parts.note: CA is the abbreviation for chartered accountant
a hoot is a very amusing person

explanation.surface: An accountant goes into business with a pair of comedians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes ... into' only joins the pieces. The answer is used in the idiom 'in cahoots'.
explanation.definitionFit: Collusion or secret alliance, as in two people working together 'in league'.

clue.text: In the position of a peer, say, abroad

indicators.note: say signals the word is heard, standing for a sound-alike spelt differently

parts.words: In the position of a peer
parts.note: to peer is to look, and one positioned to look over things is to oversee them

explanation.surface: A lord abroad finds himself in an awkward spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' suggests a lord; it is one who looks. 'say' turns OVERSEE into its sound-alike, an adjective or adverb meaning across the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Situated or going across the sea, in foreign lands, an older form of overseas.

clue.text: It's the runner's distance, but there may be some scratching

parts.note: a runner is an athlete, here in the possessive
a foot is a unit of distance, twelve inches

explanation.surface: A sprinter's race length, though a few may withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratching' suggests runners withdrawn from a race; it is itching skin.
explanation.definitionFit: The fungal infection between the toes makes sufferers itch, so it is a cause of scratching.
